info.text:
Selling your home in Canada? The gain is usually tax-free thanks to the principal residence exemption. Usually.

Example: bought for $300,000, lived there 5 years, sold for $450,000 → a $150,000 gain that can be fully exempt.

Three ways it goes wrong:
1. You still have to report the sale and designate the home (Schedule 3 + Form T2091). A late designation can cost $100 a month, up to $8,000.
2. One home per family unit, per year. Own a cottage too? Only one is covered for any given year.
3. The flipping rule (sales since 2023): sell a home you owned less than 365 days and the profit is fully taxed as business income, with no exemption, unless a life event applies (for example a death in the family or a new child joining the household).

So it's tax-free, if you report it and it was really your home.

Sources: CRA (canada.ca): principal residence, Folio S1-F3-C2, flipped property rules. The $300,000 home is an example. General information, not advice.

info.text:
Renting out a property? One deduction can bite you when you sell. 🇨🇦

Deduct now: mortgage interest (not principal), property tax, insurance, repairs, utilities.
Repair = current. Improvement = capital.
Capital costs → CCA: 4% a year on most rental buildings (half in year one), never on land. Can't create a rental loss. Optional.

The trap: $300,000 building, 10 years of full CCA = $96,395. Sell for more than you paid → $96,395 added to your income, fully taxed.

info.firstCommentText: Save this before you claim CCA 📌

info.text:
Renting out a property in Canada? Here's what you can deduct, and the one deduction that can come back when you sell.

Current expenses are deducted the same year: mortgage interest (not the principal), property tax, insurance, repairs, utilities, management fees. Your own labour isn't deductible.

Repair or improvement? Fixing a wooden step restores it: a current expense. Replacing it with concrete improves it: a capital cost.

Capital costs of the building are claimed slowly as capital cost allowance (CCA): most rental buildings are Class 1, 4% a year on the declining balance, half that in the year you buy. Never on the land. CCA can't create or increase a rental loss, and it's optional: claim any amount, or none.

The trap: example: a $300,000 building, full CCA for 10 years = $96,395 deducted. Sell the building for more than you paid, and that $96,395 comes back as recaptured CCA: added to your income in the year of sale and fully taxable (a capital gain is only half taxable).

CCA is often a deferral, not a gift. Plan before you claim.

Sources: CRA guide T4036 Rental Income; CCA for rental property; Form T776 (canada.ca). The $300,000 building is an example. General information, not advice.

info.text:
Four money moves expire on December 31 in Canada, and one deadline almost everyone gets wrong.

1. Donations: gifts made by December 31 count on this year's return. Keep the official receipt.
2. TFSA: need money early next year? Withdraw in December. The room comes back January 1, not a whole year later (withdraw in January and you wait until the next January 1).
3. FHSA: first-time home buyer? Open an FHSA before the year ends, even empty: that starts $8,000 of participation room, and unused room carries forward (up to $8,000).
4. RESP: contribute $2,500 for a child by December 31 and the basic Canada Education Savings Grant adds $500 for the year (missed years carry forward, max $1,000 of grant a year).

The myth: the RRSP deadline isn't December 31. Contributions in the first 60 days of the new year still count for this year, unless you turn 71 this year (then it's December 31).

Sources: CRA (gifts and income tax, TFSA withdrawals, FHSA participation room, RRSP important dates) and ESDC (CESG), canada.ca. General information, not advice.

info.text:
New to Canada? Your first tax return works differently. Here's what changes in year one.

1. Residency: you become a resident for tax purposes when you establish significant residential ties (a home, a spouse or partner, social ties), usually the day you arrive. Unsure? Form NR74.
2. World income: from that day you report income from every country (a tax treaty can exempt some). Foreign income earned before you arrived is generally not taxed in Canada.
3. Statement of income: you still list what you earned abroad, up to two years before, so CRA can calculate your benefits.
4. Prorated credits: most federal credits are prorated by days resident. Example: arrive September 1, 2026 → 122 days → basic personal amount ≈ $5,499 instead of $16,452.

Benefits: apply right away, before your first return: Form RC151 (GST/HST credit, now the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit) or RC66 if you have children. You need a SIN first.

Then file by April 30, every year, even with no income, or the payments stop.

Sources: CRA, Newcomers to Canada; Completing your return for newcomers; Federal non-refundable tax credits for newcomers; RC151; RC66 (canada.ca). The September example is illustrative. General information, not advice.

info.text:
New to Canada? Some government payments can start soon after you arrive, but only if you apply.

1. Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit (CGEB): it replaced the GST/HST credit on July 3, 2026. Tax-free, paid every three months (the 5th of January, April, July and October). The amount depends on your family size and income.
2. Canada child benefit (CCB): up to $8,157 a year per child under 6 (July 2026–June 2027), reduced once adjusted family net income passes $38,237. On a work or study permit? You generally need to have lived in Canada for the previous 18 months and hold a valid permit in the 19th month.

How to apply: Form RC151 (no children) or RC66 with Schedule RC66SCH (with children, also covers CGEB), or through your CRA account. You need a social insurance number.

3. Canadian Dental Care Plan: for families with no access to dental insurance and adjusted family net income under $90,000. You must be a resident and have filed a tax return.

The catch: all of them are calculated from your tax return. File every year, even with zero income.

info.text:
Own an apartment back home or savings in a foreign bank? CRA may want Form T1135, even if you owe no tax.

Who files: Canadian residents whose specified foreign property cost more than $100,000 in total, at any time in the year. Under $250,000 all year → the simplified Part A; $250,000 or more → the detailed Part B.

Counts: money in foreign bank accounts, a rental property abroad, shares of foreign companies (U.S. stocks), even held at a Canadian broker.
Doesn't count: a vacation home you use mainly yourself, property used only in an active business, and anything inside an RRSP or TFSA.

Cost, not market value. For newcomers, the cost is the fair market value on the day you became resident.

The year you become resident: no T1135. The $100,000 test starts the next year. Your world income is still reported.

Late? The penalty is the greater of $100 or $25 a day, up to $2,500 (more if the failure is knowing). It's due with your return (April 30, or June 15 if you or your spouse run a business).

Sources: CRA, Foreign Income Verification Statement; Questions and answers about Form T1135; Questions and answers about penalties (canada.ca). The couple is an example. General information, not advice.

Same $10,000 side hustle. Bigger salary. Smaller tax bill. Here's why (Manitoba, 2026).

On top of a $100,000 salary, the extra $10,000 pays federal tax at 20.5% ($2,050) and Manitoba tax at 12.75% / 17.4% ($1,688). But CPP: $0. Your job already paid the maximum CPP and CPP2 for the year, so self-employment income above it adds no contributions.

Total: $3,738. On a $60,000 salary the same $10,000 cost $4,161, including $1,190 of CPP. That's $424 less at the higher salary.

info.text:
Leaving Canada for good? CRA can tax your investments even if you never sell them. This is the departure tax (often called the exit tax).

The rule: when you become a non-resident, most property is treated as sold at fair market value on that day (and bought back at the same value). The gain is reported on Form T1243.

Example: shares outside an RRSP or TFSA bought for $40,000 and worth $100,000 when you leave → a $60,000 gain, and half of it, $30,000, is added to your income that year.

Not treated as sold: RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs and pension plans, and personal-use items worth under $10,000. Resident 60 months or less in the last 10 years? Property you owned when you arrived (or inherited after) is generally excluded, unless it's taxable Canadian property.

Paperwork: if everything you own is worth more than $25,000, list it on Form T1161. Can't pay? Form T1244 defers the tax, interest-free, until you sell; elect by April 30 of the year after you leave. Federal tax over $16,500 → CRA requires security.

When you become a non-resident depends on your ties to Canada. Plan with a professional before you go.

Sources: CRA, Dispositions of property for emigrants of Canada; Leaving Canada (emigrants); Determining your residency status (canada.ca). The couple and the shares are an example. General information, not advice.

Four expenses freelancers forget to claim, and what they're really worth.

Example: a Manitoba freelancer netting $60,000 (2026).
• Phone: 40% business use of a $960 plan = $384
• Bank and payment fees (account, card, PayPal/Stripe): $420
• Accountant (bookkeeping + the business part of the return): $600
• Business dues and licences: $250
Total: $1,654.

The honest part: a write-off isn't free money. It lowers taxable income, so this freelancer saves about 36¢ per dollar (income tax + CPP): $588.
